title: Temperature and particle motion
target: Use a particle model to distinguish average motion from total energy.
criteria: Describe temperature in terms of microscopic motion.
Use kelvin in proportional temperature comparisons.
Avoid treating a single particle speed as the temperature.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: For an ideal gas, what does absolute temperature track?
options: The color of the container.
Average translational kinetic energy per particle.
Total particle count alone.
The speed of one chosen particle exactly.
cpa.guide: In the ideal-gas model, mean translational kinetic energy is proportional to kelvin temperature.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: Two ideal-gas samples contain different numbers of the same kind of particle at the same temperature. What is equal?
options: Their average translational kinetic energy per particle.
Their total energy regardless of particle count.
Their exact particle positions.
Every particle’s instantaneous speed.
cpa.guide: Temperature relates to an average per particle, not necessarily total energy or individual speed.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: An ideal gas warms from 250 K to 500 K. What happens to average translational kinetic energy per particle?
options: It halves.
It quadruples.
It is unchanged.
It doubles.
cpa.guide: The average energy is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: An ideal gas changes from 27°C to 327°C. Use K = °C + 273. What is the ratio of final to initial average translational kinetic energy?
options: About 12.1
cpa.guide: Temperatures are 300 K and 600 K; the ratio is 2, not the Celsius ratio.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: One molecule in a gas moves faster than another at the same instant. What follows about the sample temperature?
options: All molecules must have identical speed or temperature is undefined.
The sample has two separate temperatures solely because speeds differ.
A single speed does not determine the sample’s temperature.
The slower molecule has zero kinetic energy.
cpa.guide: Particles have a distribution of speeds; temperature describes an appropriate average.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: A simulation adds more identical gas particles while keeping the same speed distribution. What happens to temperature in the ideal model?
options: It remains the same, although total kinetic energy increases.
It falls to zero.
It doubles whenever particle count doubles.
It becomes equal to the number of particles.
cpa.guide: The average energy per particle is unchanged; more particles increase the total.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.
